# PASS 1 of a tiled level — TEXTURE TILES: the floor and the walls. Opaque,
# they FILL their square edge to edge, and they REPEAT. Cut them with
#   python3 .github/art/build_tiles.py --tile texture:<raw>:<index>
# which makes them seamless; a generator will not draw a tile that repeats,
# however loudly it is asked, so the seam is fixed in the cutter, not here.
#
# Substitute {{N}} and {{ITEMS}}. Generate ONE image at 1536x1024.
# The whole standard: docs/TILED_LEVEL_STANDARD.md
#
# THE MISTAKE THAT COST A LEVEL: a game's art-style.json usually says "thick
# black outline around the whole silhouette", which is right for a character
# and catastrophic for a floor tile — every tile then carries a dark border and
# the finished level reads as graph paper. Say NO OUTLINE, NO BORDER, TEXTURE
# RUNS OFF ALL FOUR EDGES, every time.
#
# THE MISTAKE THAT COST THE SECOND LEVEL: the floor came back as fist-sized
# cobbles with bright ochre patches — correct as a picture of asphalt, and a
# loud chequered mess once each square was 32 pixels on screen with a character
# standing on it. A floor is BACKGROUND. The QUIET FLOOR and TILE-SIZED DETAIL
# paragraphs below are what stop that, and they are not optional.

A SHEET OF {{N}} SEAMLESS TEXTURE TILES for a 16-bit top-down game, drawn side
by side as {{N}} equal SQUARES in ONE image so they share a palette, a light and
a pixel scale, separated by a wide band of FLAT PURE WHITE (#FFFFFF) and with a
generous white margin all round. Each square is one MATERIAL seen from
DIRECTLY ABOVE.

CRITICAL, and the usual failure: each square is a REPEATING TEXTURE SWATCH, not
an object and not a picture. NO outline, NO border, NO frame, NO vignette and no
darkened edge around a square — the texture must run right off all four of its
edges, so that copies of the tile laid edge to edge look like one continuous
surface. No single big feature centred in a square, no obvious middle: keep the
detail small, even and spread across the whole square.

QUIET FLOOR. A floor material is the BACKGROUND of the level, never the subject.
Keep it LOW CONTRAST: one base colour plus two or three close neighbours, all
within a narrow value range, and nothing on it that jumps out — no bright
patches, no near-black stains, no strong colour accents, no bold shapes. A
character has to stand on this and stay readable, so the floor stays quieter and
darker than any character will be. Where two floor materials sit side by side in
the level they must be close in brightness; a pale material next to a dark one
turns the level into a chessboard.

QUIET IS NOT BLANK, and this is the other half of the same rule. The range is
narrow; inside it the values are SEPARATE, FLAT STEPS with hard edges — you
should be able to point at each one. A smooth, softly-blended, photographic
surface is what comes back if this is not said, and it arrives as a flat block
of colour that reads as an asset that failed to load.

TILE-SIZED DETAIL, and it is a NARROW window at both ends. Each square is going
to be shrunk to about 32 pixels across. Every feature on it must be between a
SIXTEENTH and an EIGHTH of the square wide — chunky mottled patches, short
cracks a few pixels long, the odd 2-3 pixel fleck — spread evenly, with no
obvious middle.

Too big and too small both fail, and each has cost a pass:
  * cobbles, flagstones, planks or bricks drawn a quarter of a square across
    become enormous slabs, and the level reads as a loud pattern;
  * photographic GRIT, sand, fine speckle or hairline scratches AVERAGE AWAY
    when the swatch is scaled down, and the tile arrives as a FLAT BLOCK OF
    COLOUR, which reads as an asset that failed to load.
Draw the material as if it were already only 32 pixels across: visible chunky
pixel-scale mottling in 3-4 flat values, not a photograph of a surface.

WALLS ARE THE ONE EXCEPTION TO "SEEN FROM DIRECTLY ABOVE": a wall material is
drawn FACE-ON, as the vertical surface a player looks at, so it reads as
something standing up. A wall drawn as a top view lies flat in the level and
reads as planks dropped on the ground. A wall may be higher contrast than a
floor — it is the boundary of the level and should be visible as one.

LEFT TO RIGHT: {{ITEMS}}

Chunky 16-bit pixel art on a visible coarse pixel grid: flat blocks of solid
colour, hard edges, 3-4 values per material. Draw each square as a BLOWN-UP
32x32 PIXEL IMAGE — the art pixels are big visible squares, about a thirtieth of
the square's width each, aligned to a grid, every one a single flat colour. Not
a photograph of a material, and not a smooth surface with grain sprinkled on it. No gradients, no airbrushing, no
anti-aliasing, no dithering, no noise or grain, no photographic texture. No
text, no numbers, no grid lines, no cell borders, no drop shadows, no people, no
characters.
